One famous historical example with the short-covering volume signature marked: the clearest lesson in trading other people's textbooks against them.
chapters: The most-watched pattern in the textbook — draw the head-and-shoulders every retail short is staring at, and state the setup's premise: when EVERYONE sees the top, the trade is on the other side.
Failure is fuel — walk the mechanics: the neckline break never comes, the crowded short is trapped at bad prices, and their forced covering becomes the buying power for the next leg up.
Entry over the right-shoulder high — mark the trigger, place the stop back inside the pattern, and size it through the formula — you are long the moment the pattern officially fails.
The famous one — replay the historical example with the short-covering volume signature marked bar by bar: the surge that isn't new buyers, it's trapped shorts paying any price to leave.
Trading other people's textbooks against them — close with the transferable lesson and the five-field card: the more obvious the topping pattern, the more explosive its failure.

lessons.title: Parabolic Long: Riding the Vertical, Bar by Bar
lessons.note: The runaway move managed candle by candle as the angle goes vertical — no fixed target, a pre-agreed give-back rule decided before entry, exits keyed to climax signals (largest spread, biggest gap, heaviest volume of the run). One full parabolic ridden from base to blow-off with each daily hold/trim decision narrated.
chapters: The runaway — open on a real parabolic in progress and name why every normal tool breaks here: no base, no fixed target, an angle going vertical, and a crowd in full euphoria.
The give-back rule, decided BEFORE entry — pre-commit on camera to the exact give-back that ends the trade, because the one decision you cannot make honestly mid-parabola is when to leave.

The climax checklist — the three exit signals defined and drawn: the largest spread of the run, the biggest gap of the run, the heaviest volume of the run — any of them means the crowd's last buy is in.
The full ride, narrated daily — replay one complete parabolic from base to blow-off with every daily hold-or-trim decision spoken: what the bar showed, what the rule said, what was done.
The blow-off day — the exit fires on the climax signals, the give-back rule caps the damage of imperfect timing, and the close compares what was kept versus the round-trip the euphoric holder took.

lessons.title: Parabolic Short: Shorting the Crack of a 3-5 Day Blow-Off
lessons.note: The hardest setup in the book and the true short-side mirror: a 3-5 day blow-off stretched miles above the averages, shorted only as it cracks — never into strength — with buy-stop protection above and the snap back to the 9 EMA as target, every long rule inverted on screen one at a time. States the patience rules: appears a handful of times a year, smallest size in the catalog. Artifact: the long-rules/short-rules mirror table.
chapters: The hardest setup in the book — open with the honest framing: a 3-5 day blow-off stretched miles above the averages, a handful of appearances a year, and the smallest size in the entire catalog.
Never into strength — the iron rule on a real blow-off: you short ONLY as it cracks, and every early short into the vertical is shown getting squeezed carried out on the same chart.
The mechanics — the crack entry, buy-stop protection placed ABOVE (the short side's stop is a buy), the snap back to the 9 EMA as the target, and the smallest-size rule run through the 2% formula.

The mirror, one rule at a time — invert every long rule on screen while building the long-rules/short-rules mirror table live: trigger, stop direction, target, sizing, each flipped and written into its row.
Patience is the position — close with the patience doctrine (it appears a handful of times a year; forcing it is how shorts blow up) and hand off the completed mirror table as the lesson's artifact.

lessons.title: Four-Family Placement Drill: 20 Mixed Charts
lessons.note: The setup tier's capstone gate: 20 cover-the-answer charts interleaving all four swing families — name the family, then the setup, then the entry type, before naming the trade — graded at 80% to proceed. Deliberately recycles two Winners Gallery charts from Module 2 and one regime question from Module 3, because mastery is perishable. Then the field week: one week live — scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates of this family with entry/stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome vs plan. 80% on the drill plus a completed field log opens the next family.
chapters: Why interleaved — open with the perishability point: you can ace each family in isolation and still freeze on a live chart, so this gate mixes all four swing families in one deck.

The placement sequence, demonstrated — work three charts on camera in the strict order: name the FAMILY, then the SETUP, then the ENTRY TYPE (BASE BREAKOUT / PREV DAY HIGH BREAK / PREV LOW RECLAIM / RED TO GREEN), and only then the trade.

The 20-chart deck, answer covered — run the drill guess-before-you-check, deliberately recycling two Winners Gallery charts from Module 2 and one regime question from Module 3, because mastery is perishable.
Grading and the 80% bar — score against the printed rubric on camera, and show what a miss means: not a retake-loop, but targeted remediation back to the family whose reps failed.

The field week that closes the tier — the mechanics and the pass bar: one week live, scan nightly, card 2-3 real candidates with entry and stop, log them in the Journal, grade outcome versus plan — 80% on the drill plus a completed field log opens the next tier.

modules.label: M11 · The Intraday Toolkit: Timing the Swing Entry

lessons.title: Reading the Open: ORB and the 30-Minute Pivot — Two Range-Break Timers
lessons.note: Read the first minutes of the session, then the two range-break entry timers on one replayed open: the aggressive opening-range break and its patient sibling — consolidate under the first half-hour high, break with volume. When each fits a swing entry, the pass case, and the chase case that violates both. Includes the volume-confirmation bar both timers share.
chapters: An execution timer, not a day trade — open on the trap: the swing was picked last night on the daily chart, and the only question the first 30 minutes answers is whether today puts the day's trend behind the entry.

The first minutes, replayed — run the replayed open bar by bar and narrate the auction live: the opening range drawing itself, where the volume is landing, and what a real bid looks like versus churn.

ORB, the aggressive timer — on the same replayed open, draw the opening-range high and take the break with momentum: the pass case, entry the tick it clears, and why this timer fits a swing entry only when the daily setup work was already done.

The 30-Minute Pivot, the patient sibling — mark the first half-hour's high, show price consolidating UNDER it, then the break with volume; name when patience beats aggression: gappy opens, thinner names, a YELLOW tape.

One volume bar, one chase — show the volume-confirmation bar both timers share (the break bar must expand clearly above the morning's prior bars), then the chase case that violates both — extended, mid-range, no volume — and the walk-away rule.

lessons.title: Go Signal: The Catalyst Gap That Digests into the 9 EMA, Then Engulfs
lessons.note: A catalyst gap digests into the 9 EMA, then one wide candle engulfs the pullback and closes above the catalyst high — the intraday confirmation layer for EP and Power Earnings Gap entries. One day where it fired and one where it never came, both annotated.
chapters: Why EP entries need a go signal — open with the blind-open buy that gets shaken out at the day's lows, and frame the Go Signal as the intraday confirmation layer that sits under Episodic Pivot and Power Earnings Gap entries.
The digestion into the 9 EMA — annotate the catalyst gap holding its range and drifting back into the 9 EMA on fading volume, and name it correctly: the market re-loading, not the gap failing.

The engulf above the catalyst high — freeze on the trigger bar: one wide candle that engulfs the entire pullback and closes above the catalyst high — entry there, stop under the digestion low, sized by the normal R math.
The day it fired — replay a real annotated session start to finish: gap, digestion, engulfing trigger, the fill, and where the swing stop and first target sat by the closing bell.
The day it never came — replay a real annotated session where the digestion broke the 9 EMA and the engulf never printed: the no-trade IS the win, and the card reads one line — no engulf, no entry.

lessons.title: Selling Because You Were Wrong: The Stop Is an Appointment, Not a Debate
lessons.note: Pre-commitment mechanics (hard GTC stops versus alert-and-act) and the base re-entry rule: cut at least half the moment a breakout falls back into its base. One narrated real stop-out taken exactly at plan — presented as a WIN of process — with the counterfactual computed on screen: the same trade at −2.5R when the stop gets moved once.
chapters: A different kind of sell — open on the split that organizes this whole module: selling because you were wrong is its own psychological event, and the stop is an appointment you made before the trade, not a debate you hold during it.

Pre-commitment mechanics: hard GTC versus alert-and-act — show both order setups on screen, who each style fits, and the non-negotiable they share: the exit price exists in writing before the entry order does.

The base re-entry rule — the moment a breakout falls back into its base you cut at least half, without waiting for the stop; draw the base boundary on a real chart and mark the exact bar that triggers the cut.
A real stop-out, narrated as a win — replay the actual trade taken out precisely at plan for −1R, and grade it on camera as an A trade: right size, right stop, appointment kept.
The moved-stop counterfactual — recompute the same trade live with the stop moved just once: −1R becomes −2.5R on screen, and that single number is why the appointment can never become a debate.

lessons.title: Selling Because You Were Right: Partials into Strength, Trailing into Weakness
lessons.note: Two distinct skills with two different feelings: a third off into strength at 2-3R while the crowd is euphoric, trail the remainder into weakness. The same real winner worked three ways (all-out early, all-or-nothing hold, partials) with the final R of each path compared. Artifact: the partials playbook card (first third, second third, runner rules).
chapters: Two skills, two feelings — open on the paradox: selling because you were right splits into selling into euphoria (feels too early) and holding into weakness (feels too late), and the two are trained as separate skills.

A third off into strength — the 2-3R partial taken while the crowd is euphoric: show what strength looks like on the tape, place the exact order, and explain how that sale funds the patience for everything after it.

Trailing the remainder into weakness — hand the runner to the moving average and let the market close the trade: what a normal give-back looks like, and why the trail exit always feels worse and pays better.

One winner, three ways — rework the same real winner three times on screen — all-out early, all-or-nothing hold, partials — and put the final R of each path side by side to show why partials win the long game.

The partials playbook card — close on the artifact: first-third rules (2-3R into strength), second-third rules (trail or structure break), runner rules for the piece you let run — the card members trade from.

lessons.title: The Rules Between Entry and Exit: Breakeven Rule, Trails by Timeframe, Time Stops
lessons.note: The point after which a trade must never again become a loser (roughly +1R or the first higher low); trails matched to the setup family that produced the trade — 10-day for fast movers, 10/20-day for EPs, 20/50-day for position holds, with the wrong trail's give-back quantified; and the N-day dead-money rule where nothing happening is itself the exit signal. Each rule stamped on a real chart at the bar where it fired.
chapters: Where R leaks out — open on the dead zone between entry and exit where unmanaged winners round-trip to zero, and name the three mid-trade rules this lesson installs: breakeven, trails by timeframe, time stops.
The breakeven rule — the point after which a trade must never again become a loser — roughly +1R or the first higher low — stamped on a real chart at the exact bar where the stop moves up.

Trails matched to the setup family — 10-day for fast movers, 10/20-day for EPs, 20/50-day for position holds: the trail is chosen by the setup family that produced the trade, each one stamped on a real chart at the bar it fired.
The wrong trail's give-back, quantified — run the fast mover on the slow 50-day trail and compute the give-back in R on screen, then overlay the 10-day exit bar that would have kept it.

Time stops: when nothing happening is the signal — the N-day dead-money rule stamped at the bar it fired, closing with the three rules assembled into one mid-trade checklist the member runs on every open position.

lessons.title: The Earnings Decision: Hold Through, Trim, or Step Aside
lessons.note: The most recurring swing decision the course must answer: you hold a +2R winner and it reports in three days. The mechanical rule set: check the implied move on the Calendar, compare it to your open profit cushion in R, then hold-full / trim-to-house-money / exit-and-re-enter by rule, never by feel. Two real positions worked — one held through with a cushion, one stepped aside — plus the hard rule for NEW entries inside the pre-report window.
chapters: The decision every swing trader keeps meeting — open on the live scenario: you hold a +2R winner and it reports in three days, and the answer must come from a rule set, never from feel.
Implied move versus cushion, in R — pull the implied move off the Calendar on camera and convert your open profit cushion into R, so the whole decision collapses into two numbers side by side.

The three-branch rule — cushion clears the implied move: hold full; partial cover: trim to house money; no cover: exit and re-enter by rule after the print — each branch stated as a mechanical threshold, not a judgment call.

Two real positions worked — replay one position held through with a cushion and one stepped aside, show what the report did to each, and prove both were the RIGHT call at decision time regardless of outcome.
The hard rule for new entries — no NEW position inside the pre-report window, full stop; close with the earnings-decision card: check the date, check the implied move, run the branch.

lessons.title: Two Complete Trades, Candle by Candle — Plus the Post-Exit Protocol
lessons.note: The module's mini-capstone: a winner and a loser replayed full-cycle with the sizing math, a mid-trade regime check, partial exits, and the finished journal entry for each — the loser managed exactly as well as the winner. Closes by performing the 60-second post-exit ritual (screenshot, setup tag, one-line verdict) on both exits, installing the habit before Module 14 formalizes it. Script in three chaptered segments with a micro-check between each — one recording, three sittings if needed.
chapters: The winner, sized and entered — segment one opens the mini-capstone: run the sizing math on camera (Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, under the 2% ceiling), check the regime dial, and take the entry candle by candle.

The winner, managed and journaled — partial a third at 2-3R into strength, trail the remainder into weakness, then fill in the finished journal entry on screen; micro-check one before moving to the loser.

The loser, entered with identical rigor — segment two: same sizing math, same checklist, a perfectly valid entry — then the mid-trade regime check that dims from GREEN toward YELLOW while the trade stalls.

The loser, managed exactly as well — the stop taken at plan candle by candle, and the finished journal entry graded as highly as the winner's: the outcome differed, the process did not; micro-check two.

The 60-second post-exit ritual — segment three, performed live on BOTH exits: screenshot the chart, tag the setup, write the one-line verdict — installing the habit Module 14 will formalize into the review engine.

modules.label: M13 · Portfolio Command: Sizing, Second Pass

lessons.title: Grading the Setup: A+, A, B, C — The Grade That Keys the Table
lessons.note: The rubric that turns 'I like this chart' into a letter with reasons — regime alignment, family-rubric score, RS rank, catalyst quality, cleanliness of the stop — because the firm's sizing table cannot be used until a setup has a grade. Six real candidates graded and defended live, including one seductive B that a beginner would call an A+.
chapters: Two charts, one feeling, two very different sizes — open on two real candidates the gut would size identically, then reveal the firm's sizing table and show that neither can be sized at all until it carries a letter grade.

The five rubric lines that earn the letter — walk regime alignment, family-rubric score, RS rank, catalyst quality, and cleanliness of the stop one at a time, stating what an A+ demands on each line and what drops it to a B or C.
Six real candidates, graded and defended — pull six live watchlist charts and assign each its letter on camera, naming the rubric line that decided the grade out loud before moving to the next.
The seductive B — dissect the one chart a beginner would stamp A+ and show the two lines that quietly fail it: a stop that isn't clean and an RS rank that's already fading under the pretty pattern.

No letter, no size — close by grading tonight's actual watchlist and installing the standing rule the next lesson runs on: the grade is the key that opens a cell in the sizing table, and an ungraded chart opens nothing.

lessons.title: The Table, Verbatim: GREEN+A+ = 20-25%, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, B-in-ORANGE = Skip
lessons.note: The firm's sizing table stated exactly and worked live: the same A+ setup sized on a fixed account once under GREEN and once under ORANGE with the dollar-risk difference computed, plus the universal floor restated in every cell — Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, 2% max, prefer under 1%. Includes what pulls you out of a cell mid-trade: a regime downgrade or the −5%/−10% equity triggers firing.
chapters: The table, read aloud cell by cell — put the full grid on screen and state it verbatim: GREEN+A+ = 20-25%, YELLOW+A+ = 15%, ORANGE+A+ = 8%, B-in-ORANGE = skip, and no cell is negotiable.

The floor under every cell — restate the universal law, Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance %, 2% max and prefer under 1%, then prove on screen that even a 25% GREEN+A+ position obeys it when the stop is tight.

Same A+ setup, GREEN versus ORANGE — size the identical chart on the same fixed account twice, compute shares and dollar risk both ways on camera, and let the dollar difference make the regime argument better than any speech.

What pulls you out of a cell mid-trade — walk the two evictions live: a regime downgrade while you hold, and the −5%/−10% equity triggers firing, with exactly what happens to open positions and new buys in each case.

Print it, pin it, size only from it — close with the table as the take-home artifact and the drill: re-size your last three real trades from the correct cell and log the delta between what you took and what the table allowed.

lessons.title: Portfolio Heat: All Open Risk as One Number, Capped at 10%
lessons.note: Sum of (entry − stop) × shares over equity computed on a real five-position book against the 10% aggregate heat cap, plus why 5-10 names beats 30 for momentum swing. Then the correlation check: five AI names is one trade wearing five tickers — the same book computed naive and correlation-adjusted. Artifact: the heat worksheet.
chapters: Five safe trades, one dangerous account — open with a book where every position honors the 2% ceiling individually yet the account is one bad gap from a brutal morning, and name the number that was never computed: heat.
The heat formula on a real book — compute sum of (entry − stop) × shares over equity across an actual five-position book on camera and check the result against the 10% aggregate cap.

Why 5-10 names beats 30 — make the concentration case for momentum swing: attention per name, the quality of the marginal idea, and the truth that 30 names is closet-indexing with none of the index's safety.
Five AI names is one trade wearing five tickers — rerun the same book correlation-adjusted, watch the heat number jump past the cap, and set the rule that correlated positions share one risk budget.

The heat worksheet, filled and armed — complete the artifact on the demo book, then install the nightly habit and its gate: compute your book's heat before every session, and no new buy while the number reads above 10%.

lessons.title: Progressive Exposure and the Drawdown Protocol: Pilot → Half → Full → Overweight; De-Risk at −5% and −10%
lessons.note: The confirmation-gated ladder where every rung must be paid for by the rung below — the follow-through-day pilot-buy protocol after a regime turn, expanding only after the last rung paid — and the mirror-image down-ladder: at −5% of equity halve all new sizes, at −10% pilot-or-paper only, decided now while calm because it cannot be decided during. Artifact: the signed drawdown-protocol card plus a season-long equity curve showing the ladder expanding and the protocol contracting.
chapters: One shape at three levels — open by laying the exposure ladder over a base breakout: contract, confirm, then expand is the same move at chart level, position level, and now account level, which is why full size on day one of a regime turn is a category error.

Pilot → Half → Full → Overweight, every rung paid for — teach the confirmation-gated up-ladder with the follow-through-day pilot-buy protocol after a regime turn: pilots go on first, and the next rung is bought only after the last rung's open profit is paying for it.

A real season up the ladder — narrate the season-long equity curve as pilots confirm and exposure expands rung by rung, marking on the curve exactly where each expansion was earned rather than wished for.

The mirror down-ladder, decided while calm — state the drawdown protocol verbatim (at −5% of equity halve all new sizes, at −10% pilot-or-paper only) and show the same curve's drawdown leg contracting on schedule, against the trader who tried to decide it during.

Sign the card — close by filling in and signing the drawdown-protocol card on camera with thresholds written in real dollars for the member's actual account, because a protocol you didn't pre-sign is just an opinion under stress.

modules.label: M14 · The Inner Game and the Review Engine

lessons.title: Map Your Pattern First: The Trader's Self-Diagnostic
lessons.note: The 10-question diagnostic that locates each member's dominant failure pattern (fear family, tilt family, discipline family) before any fix is offered — with the instructor mapping one of his own real historical leaks on camera. Artifact: the completed pattern map the next two lessons and the capstone read from.
chapters: You can't fix a leak you haven't found — open with two traders running the identical system to opposite P&L, and state this module's doctrine: diagnosis before any fix, self-assessment before any technique, every lesson.
The three failure families — draw the map of fear, tilt, and discipline with the signature behaviors of each, so members hear their own trading described before a single question is asked.
The 10-question diagnostic, taken live — run all ten questions on camera pause-and-answer style, showing which family each answer scores toward and why honest scoring beats flattering scoring.

The instructor's own leak, mapped — work one of my real historical failure patterns through the same diagnostic using my own journaled trades, landing on the family and the exact trigger that used to fire it.

The pattern map, completed — fill in the artifact with the member's dominant family, its trigger, and two evidence trades attached, and state the dependency out loud: the next two lessons and the capstone all read from this page.

lessons.title: FOMO and the Fear Family: Signs, Subtypes, Corrections
lessons.note: The fear emotions on one template — nature, signs, subtypes, correction — with the FOMO tax quantified from journal data (average fill vs trigger price in basis points) and the two-candle wait rule as the correction. Includes one journaled real example: the trade seen, not taken, and what the tape did after.
chapters: The FOMO tax, in basis points — open by quantifying it from real journal data, average fill versus trigger price on chased entries, so the fear has a dollar cost before it has a name.

One template for every fear — install the fixed structure (nature, signs, subtypes, correction) and run the fear family through it: FOMO, fear of loss, and fear of pulling the trigger as subtypes of the same emotion.

The trade seen and not taken — replay one journaled real example of a valid setup skipped out of fear, then roll the tape forward and read honestly what it did after, because the answer is the cure either way.

The two-candle wait rule — teach the correction mechanically: when the urgency spikes you may still take the trade, but only after two full candles close and the checklist re-passes, then show it defusing a chase on replay.

Your fear entry on the template — close with the member filling the fear-family template from their own pattern map, plus the standing measurement: log fill-versus-trigger in basis points on your next ten entries and watch your personal FOMO tax shrink.

lessons.title: Tilt and Revenge: The Circuit Breaker and the Mental Hand History
lessons.note: The tilt subtypes and one hard mechanical rule — two consecutive stop-outs = flat for the rest of the day, platform closed, no appeal — plus the next-morning re-entry protocol so the breaker never becomes a week of avoidance, and the five-step written mental hand history that dismantles a recurring mistake at its logic error. Artifact: the circuit-breaker card and one complete worked hand history.
chapters: The third trade is the expensive one — open with a real sequence where two ordinary stop-outs led to an oversized revenge trade, then name the tilt subtypes so each member can spot which one is theirs.

The circuit breaker, verbatim — state the hard rule with no softening: two consecutive stop-outs means flat for the rest of the day, platform closed, no appeal, and explain why it must be mechanical precisely because you are least rational when it fires.

The next-morning re-entry protocol — walk the specific return steps for the following open (review both stops, re-grade the setups, resume at normal size) so the breaker resets you for a day and never metastasizes into a week of avoidance.
One mental hand history, worked complete — write the five steps live on a real recurring mistake, drilling down to the logic error underneath it and the corrected logic that replaces it.

Sign the breaker, write the history — close with the two artifacts and the pass bar: the signed circuit-breaker card posted by the platform, and one complete written hand history on the dominant mistake from your pattern map.

lessons.title: The Fixed-Field Journal: Seven Fields, Three Grades — No Free-Form
lessons.note: The firm's journal schema — date, setup tag, entry type, planned R, exit-vs-plan, the three-axis grade (idea, execution, preparation), annotated screenshot — set up live in the UCT Journal, because free-form notes cannot be aggregated into diagnosis and P&L is not a grade. One winner that grades poorly and one loser that grades well, entered on camera.
chapters: Why free-form journaling fails — open with a page of eloquent free-form notes that cannot answer one aggregate question, and state the two doctrines: unstructured notes cannot be diagnosed, and P&L is not a grade.

The seven fields, one by one — walk the schema on screen (date, setup tag, entry type, planned R, exit-vs-plan, the three-axis grade, annotated screenshot) with what each field lets you aggregate later.
Set up live in the UCT Journal — build the fixed-field template inside the actual UCT Journal on camera, with setup tags matched to the catalog names so weekly stats can roll up by setup.

The winner that grades poorly, the loser that grades well — enter both real trades on camera with idea, execution, and preparation graded separately, and let the inversion land: the loss was a good trade and the win was a bad one.

Zero blank fields — close with the standing rule and pass bar: every trade journaled the day it closes, all seven fields filled, ten consecutive complete entries before the review cadence lesson has anything to review.

lessons.title: The Review Cadence: Daily Tag, Weekly Stats, Monthly Audit — Narrated on a Real Month
lessons.note: Three nested loops feeding one artifact: daily tag at exit, weekly setup-level win-rate/avg-R rollup, and an actual month reviewed end-to-end on camera — equity curve, per-setup statistics, mistake-tag frequency, converted into next month's single focus — closed by the 21-mistakes audit scored against the last 20 trades. Artifact: the 4-pillar monthly review template.
chapters: The engine that outlives the course — open with the claim this module exists to prove: three nested loops (daily tag, weekly stats, monthly audit) feeding one artifact are what turn your own trades into next month's curriculum.

The daily tag and the weekly rollup — demo the two fast loops live: the sixty-second tag at exit, then the weekly setup-level win-rate and average-R rollup that starts telling you which setups deserve your size.

A real month, end to end — narrate an actual month's review on camera in order: the equity curve, the per-setup statistics, and the mistake-tag frequency table, reading what each layer says the others can't.

One month, one focus — convert the month's data into next month's single focus item against the counter-example of the five-fix list that fixes nothing, then run the 21-mistakes audit scored against the last 20 trades to choose that focus honestly.

The 4-pillar monthly review template — close by filling the artifact (results versus target, setup-level stats, goal reflection, forward plan) from the month just reviewed, with the pass bar: one complete monthly review submitted before capstone entry.

modules.label: M15 · The Options and Flow Overlay

lessons.title: Reading the Flow Tape — and the Veto Hierarchy: Confirmation, Never Signal
lessons.note: The Options Flow tab end-to-end — sweeps versus blocks, at-the-ask aggression, and unusual-versus-baseline — with ten real prints classified on camera into signal, hedge, and noise. Then the standing order of authority: regime and chart outrank flow, always — flow can upgrade conviction on a setup you already have, but hot flow on a failed-gate chart correctly stays a no-trade.
chapters: Why flow comes second-to-last — open on a real screaming call sweep whose stock went nowhere, and name the trap this whole module exists to prevent: signal-chasing.
The anatomy of a print — walk the Options Flow tab end-to-end and define the vocabulary live on the tape: sweep versus block, at-the-ask aggression versus mid-fill, size and premium.
Unusual versus baseline — show the same $2M print landing on SPY and on a sleepy mid-cap, and teach that 'unusual' is always measured against that ticker's normal tape, never an absolute number.
Ten prints, classified live — pull ten real prints off today's tape and sort each on camera into signal, hedge, or noise, saying the tell out loud before revealing the verdict.

The veto hierarchy — state the standing order of authority (regime and chart outrank flow, always), then show hot call flow on a failed-gate chart and let it correctly die as a no-trade: flow's only legal job is upgrading conviction on a setup you already have.

lessons.title: Expressing a Swing with Calls: Strike, Expiry, Delta — Same 2% Math
lessons.note: The defined-risk stock substitute with hard rules: roughly 0.70+ delta, expiry at least twice the expected holding period, and total premium at risk inside the same risk budget the formula would have allowed for shares. One identical swing built twice — shares versus calls — with risk, breakeven, and both P&L paths compared line by line at exit.
chapters: The lottery ticket and the substitute — put a cheap OTM weekly next to a 0.70-delta three-month call on screen and name which one funds the options industry and which one is a defined-risk stock substitute.

Three hard rules — write the non-negotiables before any chain is opened: roughly 0.70+ delta, expiry at least twice the expected holding period, and total premium at risk inside the same risk budget the formula would have allowed for shares.

Same 2% math — re-run Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % for the share version of the trade, then cap total call premium at that identical dollar risk so the 2% ceiling never moves when the instrument changes.

One swing, built twice — construct the identical real swing as shares and as calls on camera: same chart, same entry and stop, contract count sized against the budget, breakeven marked on both tickets.

The exit, line by line — replay both versions to the exit and compare the P&L paths side by side on the target-hit path and the stop-hit path, showing where calls outrun stock and where theta and the premium cap bite; members leave with the call-substitution checklist.

lessons.title: Dealer Positioning and Gamma: Pins, Slingshots, and the Flow + EP Combination
lessons.note: Gamma context on the GEX view as the map of where dealers dampen versus accelerate price — one real pinned expiry and one slingshot through a level, both annotated, explicitly bounded as context for exits, never an entry system. Closes with the highest-conviction combination in the playbook: unusual call flow stacked on a qualifying Episodic Pivot, traced through all six LOOP stations.
chapters: Why price sticks to some strikes — open on an expiry-Friday chart glued to a round strike all afternoon and name the invisible hand behind it: dealer hedging.
The GEX map — read the GEX view as the map of where dealers dampen versus accelerate price: positive-gamma zones absorb moves, negative-gamma zones amplify them.
A real pin, annotated — walk one real pinned expiry bar by bar, showing dealer hedging pressing price back into the heavy strike into the close.

A real slingshot, annotated — walk one real break through a negative-gamma level that accelerated instead of stalling, then bound the tool explicitly: gamma is context for exits and targets, never an entry system.

Flow + EP, the crown combination — stack unusual call flow on a qualifying Episodic Pivot (the neglected stock gapping on a true surprise) and trace the trade through all six LOOP stations, regime to review — the highest-conviction pattern in the playbook.

lessons.title: Choose Your Two: Match the Families to Your Drill Data — and Sign the Specialization Contract
lessons.note: The member mines their own family-drill scores, placement-drill results, and journal statistics from Modules 7-14 to pick a primary family and two setups — selection by data, not preference, with the anti-hopping doctrine stated plainly: traders fail by jumping between setups, not by picking the wrong one. Ends by signing the specialization contract on camera: one primary setup, two full earnings seasons, 40 journal-logged reps before any expansion. Artifact: the family-fit scorecard and the signed contract. Uses your own logged drill and field-week results as the data — the choice is read off your numbers, not your mood. This capstone is the single graduation gate for BOTH courses (UCT Foundations points here).
chapters: The anti-hopping doctrine — open with the diagnosis that kills most traders: they fail by jumping between setups, not by picking the wrong one, so today the data picks and you commit.

Mine your own record — pull up your family-drill scores, your four-family placement-drill results, and your journal statistics from Modules 7 through 14: these logged numbers, not your mood, are the electorate.
The family-fit scorecard — fill the scorecard live on camera (accuracy per family, average R per family, reps per family) and read the primary family straight off the totals.

Two setups, chosen against preference — pick the primary and second setup inside the winning family, and work the honest case where data contradicts the heart (you love EPs, your numbers say pullbacks) — the data wins.

Sign the contract on camera — one primary setup, two full earnings seasons, 40 journal-logged reps before any expansion; the signed specialization contract plus the completed family-fit scorecard is the artifact, and this choice goes into your capstone folder — graduation itself hangs on the defended trade plan two lessons from now, the single gate both courses share.

lessons.title: Write Your Playbook: The Five-Field Entries for Your Two Setups
lessons.note: Authoring both playbook entries on the firm's five-field card, extended with your size rule and management plan — template — context and regime conditions, entry trigger, stop and size rule, management plan, failure modes — modeled by the instructor writing one complete entry live. This document is the course's terminal artifact and the thing reviewed for graduation. Authored as a real artifact in the Journal's Notebook — not a worksheet that dies in a download folder. One playbook serves both courses.
chapters: A playbook you wrote beats one you read — open with why this document is the course's terminal artifact and the thing actually reviewed for graduation, not a worksheet that dies in a download folder.

The five fields — walk the firm's template field by field: context and regime conditions, entry trigger, stop and size rule, management plan, failure modes — and the standard each must meet: numeric and falsifiable.
One entry, written live — the instructor authors a complete entry for a flagship setup in real time inside the Journal's Notebook, narrating every number as it lands on the page.

What a weak entry looks like — contrast with a vague entry ('buy strength, stop below support') and show how every unfalsifiable line becomes a mid-trade argument with yourself at the worst possible moment.

Now author yours — write both entries for your two contracted setups in the Journal's Notebook; pass bar: all five fields on both entries filled with numbers a stranger could trade from — this one document goes to graduation review and serves both courses.

lessons.title: The Trade-Plan Defense: One Full Plan Through All Six Stations, Stress-Tested
lessons.note: The graduation gate: present one complete current-market trade plan — today's dial score and GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE state, the scan source, the setup name and grade, the size from Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % and the regime × grade table, both exit paths, and the review commitment — then defend it against the standard challenge rubric. Graduation hands off to the live loop: Morning Wire as your daily scorecard, Sunday Scans as your weekly review, and the Desk as the rep room where the 40 contracted reps happen. Submitted against a published rubric with a named grader: the plan goes to the owner for async review (Compass pre-grades it), and a pass is what graduation actually certifies — for this course and for UCT Foundations, which shares this gate.
chapters: The gate, face up — put the published challenge rubric on screen first and say plainly what graduation certifies: a defended trade plan that passes a named grader's review, never percent-watched.

Stations one through four, on today's tape — build the plan live: today's dial score and GREEN/YELLOW/ORANGE state, the scan source that surfaced the name, the setup name and grade, and the size from Account Risk % = Position Size % × Stop Distance % plus the regime × grade table.

Stations five and six — write both exit paths (the wrong-path stop as an appointment, the right-path partials-and-trail plan) and the review commitment that closes the LOOP before a single share is bought.

The defense, stress-tested — run the standard challenges against the model plan on camera (gap through the stop, why this size in YELLOW, what invalidates the thesis, correlation to open positions), then show a plan failing the same rubric for contrast.

Submit and hand off — walk the submission flow (Compass pre-grades, the plan goes to the owner for async review, a pass certifies BOTH courses), then hand graduates to the live loop: Morning Wire as the daily scorecard, Sunday Scans as the weekly review, and the Desk as the rep room where the 40 contracted reps happen.
